newsitem.title: GERMANY: German leaders meet to close 1997 budget gap.
newsitem.headline: German leaders meet to close 1997 budget gap.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition met on Tuesday in Bonn to discuss how best to plug yawning gaps in Germany's 1997 budget as other officials started a three-day session to estimate the tax shortfall.
Opposition officials have said 1997 taxes could be running as much as 20 billion marks below budget projections, mainly due to high unemployment.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel contests that view, but concedes that the shortfall could be eight billion marks.
Germany, like other European nations, is under pressure to reduce its government deficit to three percent of total economic output this year, to qualify for European monetary union (EMU).
The federal budget foresees a deficit of 53.4 billion marks for 1997, in line with the EMU goal, but many observers are sceptical it can hit the mark.
Waigel has refused to exclude a spending freeze as a possible remedy, and said the government would decide appropriate measures based on the tax estimate.

Federal, state and central bank officials met with private-sector advisors in a semiannual closed-door conference in the east German town of Schwerin to hammer out hard numbers. Their results are due to be announced on Thursday.
Kohl said in a television interview this week that coalition leaders would discuss possible spending cuts and tax increases to stop the budget gap at today's talks.
"Then that will be discussed, and in all directions," Kohl said.

Peter Hintze, general secretary of Kohl's Christian Democratic Union (CDU), declined to disclose details, but said there had been a "critical development", as tax revenues were declining despite and upturn in the economy.
This underscores the need for a comprehensive reform of the tax system, as proposed by Waigel, he said.
The coalition leaders will also discuss pension reform and continued aid to east Germany, but would not hold a news conference on Tuesday as originally scheduled.
